interview_metadata.name: Harvey Lee
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: Well, I am still in my childhood, so my life story is not super long yet. I was born in Houston, Texas, and I have lived here with my mom and dad. When I was little, I liked blocks and picture books, and then I got really into LEGO because I could make whole cities and not just one building. I go to elementary school, and my favorite parts are reading time, science, art, and when we get to use computers. I like making Scratch games where a character has to dodge stuff or collect stars, and I draw characters that could be in cartoons or comic books. I play soccer with the Pine Grove Panthers in spring and fall, and on weekends I do basketball drills at the community center. Big events for me are starting school, learning Scratch, going to museums in Houston, and getting to go to the rodeo with my family.

follow_ups.question: Who has been with you for most of those important moments?
follow_ups.response: Mostly my mom and dad. My grandparents and cousins are around sometimes too, especially for cookouts or birthdays.

follow_ups.question: What is one memory that feels really important to you?
follow_ups.response: I remember finishing a big LEGO city on the living room floor with roads, a hospital, and a space tower. My dad took a picture before we had to clean part of it up.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: I think one crossroads was when I had to choose between just watching videos about games or trying to make one myself in Scratch. I saw other kids making little games, and at first I thought it looked too hard because the blocks had lots of commands. My mom said I could try for twenty minutes and stop if I hated it. I made a tiny space game where the rocket moved with arrow keys, and it did not work right at first. But then I fixed one thing, and it felt like solving a puzzle. After that I started thinking maybe I could be a game designer or animator when I grow up.

follow_ups.question: What was the hardest part of that first Scratch project?
follow_ups.response: Making the rocket not go off the screen. I had to use the edge bounce thing and change the numbers.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone help you learn it?
follow_ups.response: My teacher showed the class the basics, and my dad helped me search for a kid-friendly tutorial.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was kind of both. I chose to keep trying after it got confusing, but I also sort of fell into it because it was fun.

follow_ups.question: What made you keep going?
follow_ups.response: I wanted the rocket to move the right way, and I do not like leaving a project broken.

follow_ups.question: Do you usually stick with projects?
follow_ups.response: Yes, unless it is bedtime, and then I try to sneak one more minute.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. A school coding club or museum class would help because then I could ask questions and see other kids' projects.

follow_ups.question: What kind of class would you want?
follow_ups.response: A Scratch and animation class where we make a game with our own characters.

follow_ups.question: Where would you want that to happen?
follow_ups.response: At school, the library, or a museum because those feel easy for my family to get to.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner or children because I am nine. My mom and dad are the most important family I live with. My mom helps me with school stuff and reminds me to put my drawings in folders instead of leaving papers everywhere. My dad likes helping me build things, like when we tried making a little cardboard marble run. I also care about my grandparents because they tell stories and sometimes bring food when they visit. My cousins are fun because we can play soccer in the yard or Minecraft together.

follow_ups.question: What do you usually do with your parents on a normal evening?
follow_ups.response: Homework first, then dinner, and if there is time I draw, build LEGO, or play a little Minecraft before reading.

follow_ups.question: Who in your family do you talk to when you are upset?
follow_ups.response: Usually my mom first, but if it is about building or a game problem I ask my dad.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: No brothers or sisters live with me. My immediate family is mainly me, my mom, and my dad.

follow_ups.question: Do you wish you had siblings?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but I also like having my own LEGO sorted my way.

follow_ups.question: Do cousins feel like siblings sometimes?
follow_ups.response: A little, when they stay for a whole afternoon and we make teams.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My friends from school and soccer are important. My best school friend likes drawing monsters and robots too, so at recess we make up stories. On my soccer team, I know kids from practices on Tuesdays and games on Saturdays. My art teacher is important because she says tiny details can make a drawing feel alive. I do not have romantic partners because I am a kid.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your closest friend?
follow_ups.response: Almost every school day, mostly at recess and lunch.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your soccer friends do outside practice?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes we kick the ball around after games while parents talk.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: I live in Houston around the 77018 area. There are houses, big trees on some streets, schools, churches, little restaurants, and places where you can get tacos or barbecue. It feels busy but not like downtown. We drive a lot because Houston is spread out, but there are parks and places to ride a bike if an adult comes with me. I like that there are lots of different kinds of people and food.

follow_ups.question: Where do you like going nearby?
follow_ups.response: The park, the library, and sometimes a local museum or a place with murals.

follow_ups.question: What do you notice most when you walk or ride around?
follow_ups.response: I notice murals, big trucks, dogs, and yards that look like good places for soccer.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel mostly safe when I am with my parents. I am not allowed to go far by myself, especially near busy streets.

follow_ups.question: What makes it feel safe?
follow_ups.response: Knowing neighbors say hi and my parents know where I am.

follow_ups.question: What makes it feel less safe?
follow_ups.response: Cars going fast and being outside when it is dark.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is there is lots to do and lots of food and art. The hard part is traffic, heat, and sometimes mosquitoes.

follow_ups.question: What season is hardest?
follow_ups.response: Summer, because it gets super hot and soccer feels sweaty fast.

follow_ups.question: What would you change?
follow_ups.response: More sidewalks and more shaded places to play.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now it is me, my mom, and my dad. My parents do the grown-up things like bills, driving, groceries, and appointments. I have chores like putting away my school stuff, keeping my LEGO bins from taking over the floor, and helping set the table. Sometimes family visits, but they do not live with us.

follow_ups.question: Where do you spend most of your time at home?
follow_ups.response: The living room if I am building LEGO and my room if I am reading or drawing.

follow_ups.question: What chore do you do most often?
follow_ups.response: Clearing my plate and putting my shoes and backpack where they belong.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone who lives here is permanent.

follow_ups.question: Any long visits lately?
follow_ups.response: No, just short family visits.

follow_ups.question: Do friends sleep over?
follow_ups.response: Not usually.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes grandparents or cousins come over, but they do not usually stay overnight.

follow_ups.question: How often do they visit?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a couple times a month, more around birthdays or holidays.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when they come?
follow_ups.response: Eat together and play games or watch a movie.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, nobody is away like that.

follow_ups.question: Has that happened recently?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Is anyone away for work often?
follow_ups.response: Not for a long time.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: On school days I get up around 6:45 or 7, eat breakfast, get ready, and go to school. After school I do homework, snack, and then I might have soccer practice, drawing time, Scratch, or reading. Tuesdays are often soccer practice in season, and Saturdays can be games. On weekends I like pancakes, basketball drills, LEGO building, and sometimes family errands or a museum. Sunday night is when I have to get my backpack ready.

follow_ups.question: What is your favorite part of the week?
follow_ups.response: Saturday morning if I get pancakes and then sports or building time.

follow_ups.question: What is the busiest day?
follow_ups.response: A school day with soccer practice because I have homework and practice.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I do not have a job because I am nine. My job is basically school, homework, chores, and being on time for practices. I sometimes say my LEGO city is my work because I plan it, sort pieces, and rebuild parts when they are crooked. But I do not get paid for a real job.

follow_ups.question: What schoolwork feels most like work?
follow_ups.response: Long writing assignments and math sheets with a lot of problems.

follow_ups.question: What responsibility do you take seriously?
follow_ups.response: Bringing my homework folder back and keeping my soccer gear ready.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I have to brush my teeth, feed myself breakfast if it is cereal, keep my room sort of clean, and put library books in my backpack on library day. I also help with simple cooking sometimes, like mixing pancake batter or putting toppings on pizza. I am supposed to charge my tablet and stop using it when time is up.

follow_ups.question: What happens if your LEGO spreads out too much?
follow_ups.response: My parents tell me I need to make a path so nobody steps on pieces.

follow_ups.question: Do you cook often?
follow_ups.response: Mostly weekends, especially pancakes or helping with homemade pizza.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The main change is sports seasons. When soccer starts, I have practice and games, so there is less time for LEGO after school. When soccer is off, I do more Scratch projects or basketball drills. School also changes near testing or big projects, and my parents make bedtime stricter when I seem tired.

follow_ups.question: What do you do when you have less free time?
follow_ups.response: I save ideas in a notebook so I can build them later.

follow_ups.question: Has bedtime changed recently?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes it gets earlier if I am grumpy in the morning.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children. For me, the kid routine is school, homework, snack, then activities like soccer, drawing, reading, Scratch, or sometimes Minecraft.

follow_ups.question: What after-school activity matters most to you?
follow_ups.response: Soccer during the season and Scratch when I have a new game idea.

follow_ups.question: What do you do right after getting home?
follow_ups.response: Put my backpack down, get a snack, and usually tell my mom if something funny happened.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not had serious experiences with police. I have seen police cars at school events, traffic, and sometimes at the rodeo or big community places. Once an officer came to school to talk about safety and crossing streets. Mostly I think of them as adults who help if there is an emergency, but I also know my parents say you should be respectful and careful.

follow_ups.question: Have you ever talked directly with an officer?
follow_ups.response: Only at school, like saying hello or listening to the safety talk.

follow_ups.question: How did that feel?
follow_ups.response: Normal, because it was at school and teachers were there.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: Seeing police direct traffic after events stands out. I also notice sirens when we are driving.

follow_ups.question: Do sirens make you nervous?
follow_ups.response: A little, because I wonder what happened.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents talk about safety rules?
follow_ups.response: Yes, like staying near them and not running into the street.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not know anyone close to me who has been arrested.

follow_ups.question: Has anyone at school talked about that?
follow_ups.response: Not really, not with me.

follow_ups.question: Is it something your family discusses?
follow_ups.response: No, not much.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I cannot vote because I am nine. My parents vote, I think, and sometimes they talk about elections in grown-up voices. At school we sometimes do pretend voting, like choosing a book or class activity, and I like that because everyone gets a say.

follow_ups.question: Do you pay attention when adults talk about elections?
follow_ups.response: A little, but I usually understand only the parts about schools or parks.

follow_ups.question: What would you vote for if kids could vote on local things?
follow_ups.response: More playground shade, better school lunches, and more library books.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I do not really have grown-up political views yet. I think people should be kind, kids should be safe, schools should have good books and art supplies, and parks should be clean. I also think museums and libraries are important because kids can learn things there even if they do not have a lot of money. When I hear adults argue, I do not always know what side is what. I mostly think about fairness, helping people after storms, and making sure kids do not get bullied.

follow_ups.question: Where do those ideas come from?
follow_ups.response: My parents, teachers, books, and noticing when something feels unfair at school.

follow_ups.question: What public problem do you understand best?
follow_ups.response: Maybe schools needing supplies or parks needing to be safer and cleaner.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I do not think I have political views that change like adults. I have started noticing more that grown-up decisions affect kids. Like if a park is closed, or school has fewer supplies, or there is traffic near school, kids feel it too. I guess I have become more curious about who decides those things.

follow_ups.question: What made you notice that?
follow_ups.response: School announcements, parent conversations, and seeing signs around election time.

follow_ups.question: Do you ask questions about it?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but if the answer gets too long I get confused.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have heard about racism and Black Lives Matter from adults and sometimes school lessons about treating people fairly. I do not understand everything about policing, but I understand that people should not be treated badly because of their skin color. Houston has lots of different people, so it feels important to be respectful. It affects me mostly by making me ask questions and think about fairness.

follow_ups.question: Have teachers talked about race at school?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes in history or kindness lessons, usually in a careful way.

follow_ups.question: How do you think kids your age understand it?
follow_ups.response: We understand fairness and bullying more than big policy words.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think the main thing is people wanting to be safe and treated fairly. I know I am still a kid, so I mostly think about it like, if someone is scared or hurt, adults should listen. I also think names and stories matter because people are not just news. I do not go to protests, but I can understand why people want others to pay attention.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about it with friends?
follow_ups.response: Not a lot. Kids usually talk about games, sports, and school stuff.

follow_ups.question: What would fairness look like at school?
follow_ups.response: Teachers listening to everyone and not assuming someone did something wrong.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think America has many kinds of people, and Houston shows that because I hear different languages and see different foods and festivals. I also know from school that history had unfair things like slavery and segregation. It seems like some unfair things did not just disappear. I think kids should learn about it honestly but also learn how to be friends and work together.

follow_ups.question: What helps you learn about different cultures?
follow_ups.response: Food, festivals, books, school projects, and neighbors.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable asking questions?
follow_ups.response: Usually with my parents or teachers, yes.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: I mostly listen and ask my parents questions. I have not joined protests or posted about it.

follow_ups.question: What kind of questions do you ask?
follow_ups.response: I ask why people are marching or why something on the news happened.

follow_ups.question: Do you keep your thoughts private at school?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, unless a teacher brings it up.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My parents talk about fairness and being respectful. They do not put a lot of heavy news in front of me, but if I ask, they answer. Some adults in my family talk more about it when they think kids are not listening. My teachers mostly talk about kindness, history, and everyone belonging.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents ever disagree about these topics?
follow_ups.response: Maybe, but not in a big yelling way around me.

follow_ups.question: Who explains hard topics best?
follow_ups.response: My mom, because she uses examples from school or friends.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: I am pretty healthy. I play soccer, do basketball drills, and run around outside when it is not too hot. I get normal kid colds sometimes, and I have allergies sometimes when pollen is bad. I go to the doctor for checkups and shots. I need reminders to go to bed because I can stay up drawing or building.

follow_ups.question: What helps you feel your best?
follow_ups.response: Enough sleep, not too much screen time, and eating breakfast.

follow_ups.question: What makes you feel bad?
follow_ups.response: Too much heat, allergies, or staying up too late.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Sports make it easy because running is part of the game. My parents make healthy dinners, but I would choose pizza a lot if I could. It is hard when it is hot outside or when I want to keep playing on the tablet instead of sleeping.

follow_ups.question: What healthy food do you actually like?
follow_ups.response: Avocado cucumber sushi rolls, fruit, and cucumber slices.

follow_ups.question: What unhealthy food is hardest to resist?
follow_ups.response: Pepperoni pizza with extra mozzarella.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing really big. I have not broken a bone. I had a bad cough once and had to miss a couple days of school, and allergies bother me sometimes. I have had scrapes from soccer and bumping into things, but nothing huge.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed activities because of health?
follow_ups.response: Only when I was sick or if allergies made me feel gross.

follow_ups.question: Any regular medicine?
follow_ups.response: Not regular medicine except allergy stuff if my parents say I need it.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Health does not usually get in my way except when I am sick and have to miss school or practice.

follow_ups.question: What is hardest when you miss school?
follow_ups.response: Catching up on worksheets and missing recess with friends.

follow_ups.question: Do injuries affect sports?
follow_ups.response: Only little scrapes or sore legs.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Not in a very big way. Sometimes grandparents have appointments, and adults talk about blood pressure or medicine, but I do not know all the details. If someone is sick, we might bring soup or call them. It makes me worry a little, but my parents usually say they are being taken care of.

follow_ups.question: How do you help when someone is sick?
follow_ups.response: I draw a card or try to be quieter.

follow_ups.question: Do health worries change family plans?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes visits get moved if someone is not feeling well.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: My parents handle that. I go to a regular doctor and dentist, and sometimes we wait in the waiting room a long time. I do not think I have had to skip care I needed. I know appointments can be annoying because they interrupt school or activities.

follow_ups.question: What do you bring to appointments?
follow_ups.response: A book, sketchpad, or sometimes the tablet.

follow_ups.question: Do you feel comfortable at the doctor?
follow_ups.response: Mostly, except shots make me nervous.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: We mostly use regular doctors. At home, if I have a sore throat, my parents might give me warm tea with honey or soup. For stuffy nose, sometimes steam from a shower helps. I do not think we use special alternative medicine.

follow_ups.question: What home remedy do you like?
follow_ups.response: Honey in warm tea because it tastes good.

follow_ups.question: Who decides when you need a doctor?
follow_ups.response: My mom and dad.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: No, I am nine, so I do not smoke or drink alcohol. If I am upset, I draw, build LEGO, read, or talk to my parents. Sometimes I listen to movie music because it makes things feel like an adventure instead of just a bad day.

follow_ups.question: What do you draw when you are upset?
follow_ups.response: Usually a superhero, robot, or creature with armor.

follow_ups.question: What music helps?
follow_ups.response: Hans Zimmer or John Williams soundtracks.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or anything like that. If I am sick, my parents give me kid medicine like for fever or allergies, but only when I need it. The most recent was probably allergy medicine when my nose was itchy.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever take medicine by yourself?
follow_ups.response: No, my parents handle it.

follow_ups.question: How do you cope without medicine?
follow_ups.response: Resting, drawing, and drinking water.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: My parents pay for it and use insurance, I think. I do not know the money details. For me, health care is mostly checkups, dentist visits, shots, and getting medicine if I am sick. My job is to cooperate even if I do not like shots.

follow_ups.question: Do your parents talk about cost?
follow_ups.response: Not much in front of me.

follow_ups.question: What health care visit do you dislike most?
follow_ups.response: Shots at the doctor.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I do not like shots, but I know vaccines are supposed to keep people from getting really sick. My parents decide and keep me up to date.

follow_ups.question: What helps you get through a shot?
follow_ups.response: Looking away and thinking about something else.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust vaccines?
follow_ups.response: Yes, because my parents and doctor say they help.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: For me, trusted sources are my parents, my doctor, and school nurses or teachers. I do not look up vaccine stuff by myself. If I hear something confusing, I ask my mom or dad.

follow_ups.question: Do you watch vaccine news?
follow_ups.response: No, not really.

follow_ups.question: Who explains medical things clearly?
follow_ups.response: My doctor and my mom.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Most of the time I have felt good and busy. I get excited when I have a new project, like a LEGO city or Scratch game. I also get frustrated if something breaks or if I have to stop in the middle because it is bedtime. Sometimes school feels tiring, especially if there is a big test or a lot of homework. I feel happiest when I have time to make things and when my family is not rushing.

follow_ups.question: What feeling do you have most often?
follow_ups.response: Excited or curious, but sometimes annoyed when I have to clean up.

follow_ups.question: What helps you calm down?
follow_ups.response: Drawing, reading, or sorting LEGO pieces.

transcript.question_text: Tell me a story about a time in the last year when you were in a rough place or struggling emotionally.
transcript.response: One time I had a school project and a soccer game close together, and I felt like I could not finish everything. I got upset because my poster did not look like the picture in my head. My mom helped me make a list: finish the title, glue the pictures, then write three facts. After that it felt smaller. I still was tired, but I finished it.

follow_ups.question: What did you learn from that?
follow_ups.response: Breaking it into steps helps more than just staring at the whole project.

follow_ups.question: Did anyone at school notice?
follow_ups.response: My teacher said the poster was organized, which made me feel better.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they struggle with depression, anxiety, or something else like that. How about for you?
transcript.response: I do not think I have depression or anything diagnosed. I do worry sometimes about tests, messing up in soccer, or being late. I can get nervous before presenting in class. Usually it goes away after I start doing the thing.

follow_ups.question: What does nervous feel like for you?
follow_ups.response: My stomach feels weird and I talk faster.

follow_ups.question: Who helps when you worry?
follow_ups.response: My parents or my teacher if it is at school.

transcript.question_text: How has it been for your family?
transcript.response: My family has been mostly okay, but grown-ups get stressed about work, bills, traffic, and schedules. I can tell when everyone is rushing.

follow_ups.question: What does family stress look like at home?
follow_ups.response: Shorter answers, more reminders, and everyone trying to get out the door.

follow_ups.question: What helps the family mood?
follow_ups.response: Dinner together, weekend pancakes, or watching a movie.

transcript.question_text: Some people say that religion or spirituality is important in their lives, for others not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: Religion is part of my life some, but I am still figuring out what I think. My family sometimes goes to church for holidays or with relatives, and we talk about being kind and thankful. I know some prayers from family times, but I do not know all the grown-up beliefs. I think it is important to be good to people and help neighbors. I also like science, space, and asking questions, and my parents say questions are okay.

follow_ups.question: Do you identify with a religion?
follow_ups.response: Christian, kind of because that is what my family is around, but I am still a kid.

follow_ups.question: When do you notice religion most?
follow_ups.response: Holidays, family meals, and when relatives talk about church.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they use Facebook, Instagram, or other social media to stay connected with the wider world. How about for you? Tell me all about how you use these types of platforms.
transcript.response: I do not have my own Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter because I am nine. summaries.demographer: Harvey Lee is a 9-year-old Asian American boy living in Houston, Texas, with both parents in a three-person household, with no spouse, children, lodgers, or temporary residents (Q51-Q55, Q84, Q88-Q89). He is enrolled full time in public elementary school and has completed less than ninth grade, with school serving as his primary institutional setting (Q90-Q92). His household appears stable and parent-supported, though he has limited knowledge of adult finances, taxes, insurance, and parental education details (Q56-Q64, Q74-Q76, Q100-Q107). He identifies loosely as Christian through family context and speaks mostly English at home (Q47, Q88, Q94).
summaries.behavioral_economist: Harvey shows strong future orientation for a child, saving birthday or gift money for LEGO, books, and art supplies while learning to delay purchases and distinguish wants from needs (Q60-Q64, Q83). His choices are motivated by creative payoff, mastery, and visible progress, as seen in persisting with Scratch debugging and breaking school projects into steps (Q02-Q03, Q44, Q50). He responds to constraints such as bedtime, screen-time limits, sports schedules, and family budgets by planning in notebooks or reusing existing materials (Q17-Q18, Q48, Q60). Peer and adult encouragement matter: teachers, parents, and teammates shape his participation in art, coding, schoolwork, and sports (Q04-Q07, Q106).
summaries.political_scientist: Harvey is pre-voting age and has no party identification, but he has an emerging civic frame organized around fairness, schools, parks, libraries, safety, and kindness (Q23-Q24, Q95-Q96). His institutional trust is child-centered: he trusts parents, teachers, doctors, and school adults more than abstract political systems (Q30, Q42). On race, racism, Black Lives Matter, and policing, he expresses age-appropriate awareness through fairness and anti-bullying language rather than adult policy positions (Q26-Q30). His community attachment is local and experiential, rooted in Houston's multicultural food, festivals, parks, museums, traffic, heat, and neighborhood life (Q08-Q10, Q28).
summaries.psychologist: Harvey presents as imaginative, conscientious, curious, and organized, with a strong maker identity built around LEGO, drawing, Scratch, science, and storytelling (Q01-Q04, Q65, Q108). He regulates frustration through drawing, building, reading, music, lists, and parental support rather than substances or social media (Q38-Q39, Q43-Q45, Q49-Q50). His self-concept combines creativity and competence: he likes solving problems, preserving project ideas, and being taken seriously even as a child (Q02-Q03, Q18, Q109). Emotionally, he reports normal child worries about school, tests, presentations, bedtime, and performance, with no diagnosed depression or anxiety in the interview evidence (Q43-Q46).
